The duplex is laid out with two bedrooms up stairs with a bathroom in the middle. Downstairs is the living room, kitchen, dining room and roomates room and her own bathroom. When we picked rooms I picked first because I moved in first and then my roommate upstairs picked and then the girl downstairs. She wasn’t too happy with her room because it was the smallest and the location but settled because she had her own bathroom. So the roommate downstairs has a very weird schedule. So obviously with the constant changing work schedule her sleeping schedule has became very weird and erratic and we never know when she’s asleep now. So since I can never guess when she’s asleep I often so downstairs in the kitchen and make food and play music on my speaker while I meal prep. It’s apart of my routine through out the day that i really enjoy since I don’t work till 2pm. But yesterday my roommate downstairs texted our group chat and asked us to please stop playing music in the kitchen at any time of the day. She said it wakes her up almost every time and when she is a wake it’s just very disruptive. My other roommate said sure but I said that’s not really fair because she often plays music too in the kitchen. She told me it wasn’t really fair that she had the shittiest room in the house and that if I wanted to switch with her so she wouldn’t have to be woken up by it that would be fine. Of course I said no and said I was going to keep playing music because it’s noon usually when I do it and it’s ridiculous I have to step around her schedule. Both my roommates are saying I’m being an asshole and that it’s the least I can do because I have the best room in the house because it’s the most separate. I honestly think they are being assholes because why should I have to be so quiet I’m the middle of the day!?

Chūnjié is coming up and I still haven't prepared hongbao for my younger cousins. How would you handle that?

No worries! Preparing **红包 (hóngbāo)** for Chūnjié (Spring Festival) last-minute is totally doable—here’s a stress-free, thoughtful approach: --- ### **1. Quick & Practical Hongbao Ideas** **A. Cash Hongbao (Traditional & Safe)** - **Amount:** Follow local customs (e.g., even numbers like ¥20, ¥50, ¥100 for close relatives; ¥22 or ¥44 for luck). Avoid odd numbers or ¥4 (sounds like "death" in Mandarin). - **Packaging:** - **Red envelopes (红包袋):** Buy pre-made ones at supermarkets (e.g., Walmart, Costco) or online (Taobao, Amazon). Look for **gold/red foil** for extra festivity. - **DIY:** Use red paper (available at craft stores) + glue/stickers. Add a **gold seal (印章)** or calligraphy for a personal touch. - **Alternative:** Use **red envelopes with QR codes** (e.g., WeChat Pay/Alipay) for digital hongbao (if your cousins are tech-savvy). **B. Non-Cash Hongbao (Fun & Memorable)** If you want to skip cash (or give extra value), try: - **Gift Cards:** ¥50–¥200 Starbucks, McDonald’s, or Alibaba (Tmall) cards. Kids love these! - **Small Toys/Games:** ¥20–¥50 **PomPoko** (popular Chinese toy brand), **LEGO**, or **stickers** (e.g., Disney, Hello Kitty). - **Food Coupons:** Vouchers for their favorite snacks (e.g., "¥30 for a box of Mooncakes" or "¥50 for a meal at [local restaurant]"). - **Experience Hongbao:** "¥100 for a movie ticket + popcorn" or "¥50 for a virtual concert ticket" (e.g., Bilibili or Tencent Music). - **Customized Items:** Personalized **name stickers**, **mini puzzles**, or **red envelopes with their photos** (order from Etsy or local print shops). **C. Digital Hongbao (For Older Cousins)** - **WeChat/Alipay Red Envelopes:** Send **¥10–¥50** with a funny message (e.g., "For your future success! 🎉"). Add a **GIF** or **sticker** to make it special. - **Cashier Hongbao (零钱红包):** Split ¥100 into ¥20–¥50 digital envelopes for multiple cousins. --- ### **2. Last-Minute Tips** - **Buy in Bulk:** Supermarkets (e.g., Carrefour, H Mart) or **Taobao** often have red envelopes in packs. Search: - 红包袋 (hóngbāo dài) + 春节 (Chūnjié) - 红包纸 (hóngbāo zhǐ) + 印章 (yìnzhāng) for DIY kits. - **Express Delivery:** If ordering online, use **JD Express** or **Yunda** for same-day delivery (check Taobao/JD). - **Wrap It Nice:** Add a **red ribbon**, **gold washi tape**, or a **handwritten note** (e.g., "祝你新年快乐！" *Zhù nǐ xīnnián kuàilè!* = Happy New Year!). - **Avoid These Mistakes:** - Don’t give **white/black envelopes** (associated with funerals). - Skip **odd amounts** (e.g., ¥15) or ¥4 (bad luck). - Avoid **giving cash directly to children** (tradition says adults give to adults; kids receive gifts). --- ### **3. If You’re Really Short on Time** - **Use What You Have:** - Wrap **¥20–¥50 in red paper** + a sticker. - Give **a small toy + ¥10** (e.g., a keychain + cash). - **Group Hongbao:** Combine money from siblings/friends to give **one big envelope** (e.g., ¥200 total split among cousins). - **Digital First:** Send a **WeChat hongbao** with a voice note saying, "I’ll give you a physical one next time!" --- ### **4. Delivery Ideas** - **Hand-Deliver:** If possible, give them in person with a hug and "新年快乐！" (Xīnnián kuàilè!). - **Post It:** Use **China Post** (if they’re far) or **JD Courier** (fast and reliable). - **Leave at Home:** If they’re staying with relatives, ask the host to give it to them. --- ### **5. Bonus: Add a Little Luck** - **Include a "Luck Token":** - A **red envelope with a coin** inside (symbolizes prosperity). - A **small "福" (fú = luck) charm** or **mandarin orange** (symbolizes wealth). - A **handwritten fortune** (e.g., "This year, you’ll get an A+ in exams!"). --- ### **Example Checklist (1-Hour Prep)** | Task | Where to Get It | Cost (Approx.) | |--------------------|--------------------------|----------------| | Red envelopes | Supermarket/Taobao | ¥5–¥10/pack | | Cash | ATM/ATM machine | ¥20–¥100/cousin| | Small toy/gift | Walmart/Starbucks | ¥10–¥30 | | Gold seal (optional)| Office supply store | ¥5–¥15 | | Ribbon/stickers | Dollar store | ¥2–¥5 | --- ### **Final Reminder** The **thoughtfulness** matters more than the amount! Even a **handmade envelope with ¥20 and a smile** will make them happy. If you’re still unsure, **digital hongbao** is the safest bet. **祝你包红包顺利！** (Zhù nǐ bāo hóngbāo shùnlì! = Wish you smooth hongbao-giving!) prediction.raw: This is a **nuanced** situation, and whether you’re "AITA" depends on **context, fairness, and communication**—not just the absolute loudness of the music or the time of day. Here’s a breakdown of the ethical and practical angles, along with a **0/1 rating** for your specific question (though I’d argue it’s more about *degrees* of responsibility): --- ### **Rating: 0.3/1 (Borderline "Not AITA," but with major flaws)** *(If we’re scoring on a scale where 0 = "You’re a saint" and 1 = "You’re a jerk," this lands closer to 0.3—meaning you’re not *intentionally* malicious, but your approach lacks empathy and accountability.)* --- ### **Why It’s Not Just About "Middle of the Day"** 1. **Sleep Disruption ≠ Just Noise Pollution** - Your roommate’s erratic schedule isn’t a complaint about *loudness*—it’s about **invasiveness**. For someone with irregular sleep, even **low-volume music** (e.g., podcasts, soft tunes) can disrupt their rest if it’s unpredictable. This isn’t about "being woken up" like an alarm; it’s about **fragmented sleep**, which is physically taxing. - *Example:* Imagine someone who sleeps during the day but works nights. If you play music at 11 AM *every day*, they might never get a full nap, leading to chronic fatigue. 2. **The "Best Room" Argument is a Red Herring** - You’re right that your room is more private (upstairs), but **privilege doesn’t grant you immunity from basic decency**. The duplex layout is fixed, but **how you use shared spaces** (kitchen/living room) is negotiable. - Your roommate’s room is smaller and less private, but **she’s not asking for a room upgrade—she’s asking for basic consideration**. That’s not unreasonable. 3. **Your Routine vs. Her Needs** - You frame music as a "routine you enjoy," but **routines can be adjusted**. If you’re not working until 2 PM, you could: - Play music **only when you’re alone** (e.g., no one’s around). - Use **headphones** when in shared spaces. - Lower the volume or switch to **instrumental/white noise** (less jarring). - **Ask her schedule** (even if it’s irregular) and avoid music during her known "rest windows." 4. **The "Fairness" Counterargument Fails** - You said: *"She plays music too!"* But: - **Frequency/Volume:** Does she play music *constantly* like you do? Or is it occasional? - **Impact:** Does her music disrupt *your* sleep? If not, the comparison is unfair. - **Intent:** You’re **deliberately** using the kitchen as a personal entertainment hub during the day. Her music might be background noise, but yours is a **shared-space ritual**. 5. **The "Switch Rooms" Offer is a Power Move** - She’s not asking for a trade—she’s saying, *"If you’re unwilling to compromise, at least acknowledge the imbalance."* Your refusal to even consider it shows **defensiveness**, not reasonableness. --- ### **Where You’re *Partially* Right** - **It’s Not Always Noon:** If she’s **consistently** disrupted by music at 11 AM, but not at 3 PM, that’s a clue her issue isn’t just "anytime." But even then, **some flexibility** is needed. - **Your Roommate’s Support:** If your other roommate agrees with you, it *could* suggest she’s also affected—but you didn’t mention if she’s ever complained. If she hasn’t, that’s a sign your issue might be more personal. --- ### **How to Fix This (Without Being a Doormat)** 1. **Apologize for the Disruption** - Acknowledge: *"I realize my music is affecting your sleep, and I’m sorry. I’ll try to be more mindful."* - **Don’t** say *"But you play music too!"* (it’s not the same). 2. **Propose a Compromise** - *"Can we agree on a ‘quiet hours’ window when I avoid music, even if it’s not your exact sleep time?"* - *"I’ll use headphones or lower the volume when I know you’re around."* 3. **Respect Her Schedule (Even If It’s Weird)** - If she texts you her work schedule, **check it before playing music**. If she doesn’t, ask: *"Do you want me to avoid music during certain times?"* 4. **Address the Underlying Issue** - If she’s **chronically sleep-deprived**, this might be a sign of a larger problem (e.g., shift work + no recovery time). A simple *"Hey, how’s your sleep been lately?"* could open a conversation about support. --- ### **Why Your Roommates Are Angry (And You’re Missing the Point)** They’re not mad because you’re "being loud"—they’re mad because: - **You’re prioritizing your comfort over theirs** without considering the impact. - **You’re dismissive of their needs** ("it’s ridiculous I have to step around her schedule"). - **You’re using the "best room" as a shield** to avoid accountability. --- ### **Final Verdict** You’re **not a terrible person**, but you’re **acting like one** in this situation. The fact that you’re debating whether you’re "AITA" instead of **actively solving the problem** shows a lack of empathy. **A mature adult would:** 1. **Admit the issue** (you’re disrupting her). 2. **Offer a solution** (adjust your routine). 3. **Follow through** (don’t double down). **Score: 0.3/1** because you’re not *maliciously* wrong, but you’re **actively ignoring the problem** in a way that’s selfish and inconsiderate. **Fix it now before it escalates.** --- ### **TL;DR** - **No, it’s not "ridiculous" to adjust your routine** for someone with a weird sleep schedule. - **Yes, you owe her an apology and a compromise.** - **No, your room’s layout doesn’t give you a free pass to be inconsiderate.** - **Do better.** People remember how you treat those who can’t fight back.
